evidence.label: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False
Lean doc (weaker counting bound formalized)
evidence.note: Lean proves exact counting for canonically encoded k-CNF in time (L+1)^{O_k(1)}2^{O_k(n(log log n)²/√log n)} with polynomial space, matched to one Comparator statement. The paper's sharper bound and corollaries are not in the scope note.

headline: A claimed algorithm that solves 3-SAT in subexponential time, which would make the Exponential Time Hypothesis false.
scope: The claim is a deterministic exact-counting algorithm for k-CNF with fixed k. It runs in time 2^(n/(log n)^(1/2+o(1))) up to polynomial factors.
plain: A SAT formula is a list of rules on true-or-false switches. Since 2001, many results assumed the Exponential Time Hypothesis: 3-SAT needs time that grows exponentially in the number of switches. This paper claims a method that counts every satisfying setting faster than that. If it holds, ETH and its stronger forms are false.
doesNot: This does not give subexponential algorithms for every NP problem, and it is not a practical fast SAT solver.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who stated ETH
scorecard.significanceWhy: If it holds, it overturns a hypothesis behind many hardness results in algorithms and complexity.

explanation:
Start with a small puzzle. A 3-CNF formula is a list of rules on true-or-false switches. Each rule is an OR of three conditions, such as "x₁ is true or x₂ is false or x₅ is true". An assignment sets every switch. It satisfies the formula if every rule holds. With n switches there are 2ⁿ assignments, so checking them all takes about 2ⁿ steps. For n = 100 that is about 1.27 × 10³⁰.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis, or ETH, said that 3-SAT needs 2^Ω(n) deterministic time in the worst case[4]. In plain words, the exponent must grow in proportion to n. Faster methods existed, but they only shrank the constant in the exponent. Schöning's method is a random search[20]. It runs in about (4/3)ⁿ time for 3-SAT[8]. That is about 2^(0.415n). Liu's deterministic method runs in O(1.32793ⁿ) time[9]. Exact counting was harder still. Earlier counting methods took 2^(n − Ω(n/k)) time for fixed k ≥ 3[10]. Impagliazzo and Paturi stated ETH in 2001, and many hardness results in algorithms then assumed it.

The paper claims a deterministic method that counts the satisfying assignments of any k-CNF exactly, for each fixed k ≥ 2[1]. Here m is the number of rules. Its time is (n + m)^O(1) × 2^O(n log log n / √log n), with constants that depend on k. It uses only polynomial memory[2]. When m ≤ Dn for a fixed D, the bound improves to a polynomial times 2^O(n / √log n)[3]. A count above zero means the formula is satisfiable[6]. So the method also decides 3-SAT in 2^o(n) time, which ETH ruled out[5].

How large is the saving? Take n = 1,000,000. The natural log of n is about 13.8, and its square root is about 3.72. In the fixed-density case the exponent is n / √log n, about 269,000. Ignoring the hidden constants, that is about a quarter of n. The general bound has an extra log log n factor, about 2.6 here. The constants depend on k and are not stated, so this is a statement about growth, not a fast program. As n grows, the ratio to n keeps shrinking. That is what subexponential means.

The proof first treats a 3-CNF in which each switch appears in at most three rules. Each rule becomes a polynomial, and their product has degree at most 3n. Interpolation then recovers the exact count from sums over small groups of switches[14]. A splitting step called sparsification, plus copying of switches, extends this to every k-CNF[15].

The paper lists consequences. It also refutes the strong and gap forms of ETH and the nondeterministic form NSETH[5]. It refutes the counting form #ETH[11]. It gives subexponential near-optimal methods for Max-k-SAT[16], and subexponential counting of independent sets and colourings[13]. It gives a circuit lower bound for the class E^NP[12]. It does not give subexponential time for every NP problem, because such run times do not carry through general reductions[7]. The circuit bound is not a superpolynomial bound for NP[18]. It does not conflict with known exponential lower bounds for restricted proof systems such as regular resolution[17].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked exact counting for k-CNF formulas in a fixed input format. Its time bound is slightly weaker, with (log log n)² in place of log log n. That still refutes ETH. One Comparator statement fixes what Lean had to prove. The sharper bound in the paper and the corollaries are not in the Lean scope note. No independent review of the proof has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the proof holds, since it overturns ETH. Lean checks a slightly weaker bound on a fixed input format, which still refutes ETH. No independent review is published.

glossary.meaning: A formula made of rules, each an OR of at most k conditions on true-or-false variables.
A setting of all the variables that makes every rule true.
The conjecture that 3-SAT needs time 2 to the power of a constant times n.
Running time whose exponent grows slower than any constant times n.
Memory that grows at most like a fixed power of the input size.
Splitting a formula into many formulas with few rules per variable, without losing solutions.
Recovering a polynomial's value from its values at other points.
